title: Controv. XII: Does baptism regenerate infants inwardly, bind the Spirit to the water, and admit lay or even women baptizers in necessity?
pass_a_gloss: XII. On Baptism. Is the efficacy of holy Baptism such that as many infants as are baptized with water are by that very fact inwardly regenerated by the Holy Spirit, from which it would follow that they have actual faith, since Baptism profits nothing without faith? Is the washing of Baptism not only an external means divinely ordained, into a Sacrament or symbol and seal of our Regeneration (Titus 3:5; Acts 16:22), and also a moral instrument of it, under the condition of faith — either present in adults (Mark 16:16) or to follow as regards infants who will live — having from this a hypothetical necessity and the necessity of the divine precept: but is it also a physical means and an inward efficiency without which regeneration does not ordinarily take place, and by which that same regeneration is altogether effected, having from this an absolute necessity and the necessity of a means without which not? So that the mere deprivation of Baptism in infants, if it does not damn, at least places them in danger of damnation, and Christ's words about regeneration from water and Spirit (John 3:5) make for this. Whence in a case of necessity may even private persons commonly called laypeople, and even women, not indeed also preach (1 Corinthians 14:34–35), but nevertheless be allowed to baptize? The Lutherans affirm; the Reformed deny.
pass_b_english: Controv. XII. On Baptism. Is holy Baptism so effective that every infant washed with water is by that very act inwardly regenerated by the Holy Spirit — and so must have actual faith, since baptism profits nothing without faith?

Is baptism's washing only an outward means God ordained, a sacrament or symbol and seal of our regeneration (Titus 3:5; Acts 16:22), and a moral instrument of it, under the condition of faith — faith already present in adults (Mark 16:16), or faith still to come in infants who will live — and so necessary only hypothetically, as a divine command?

Or is it also a physical means and an inward efficiency without which regeneration does not ordinarily happen, and by which that regeneration is altogether worked — and so absolutely necessary, a means without which it cannot be?

On that reading, mere lack of baptism in infants, if it does not damn them outright, at least puts them in danger of damnation; and Christ's words about being born of water and Spirit are pressed that way (John 3:5).
From this they ask whether, in necessity, private persons ordinarily called laypeople — and even women — may baptize, though they may not preach (1 Corinthians 14:34–35).
The Lutherans say yes; the Reformed say no.
source_text: XII. De Baptismo. An S. Baptismi ea sit efficacia, ut quoquot Infantes aquâ baptizantur, hoc ipso internè regenerentur per Spiritum S. unde sequatur eos habere fidem actualem, quum Baptismus nihil profit fine fide? An sit adeò Baptismi lavacrum non solummodo medium externum divinitus ordinatum, in Sacramentum vel symbolum ac figillum nostrae Regenerationis, Tit. III.5. Act. XVI.22. ut & Instrumentum illius morale; sub conditione fidei vel praesentis in adultis, Marc. XVI.16. vel secuturae quoad victuros Infantes; habens hinc necessitatem hypotheticam & praecepti divini: Verum etiam an sit medium physicum, & efficientia interna, sine quo non fiat ordinariè Regeneratio; & quo omnino eadem efficiatur, habens hinc necessitatem absolutam & medii sine quo non? Ita ut sola privatio Baptismi in infantibus si non damnet, certe in damnationis periculo constituat, & huc faciant verba Christi de regeneratione ex aqua & spiritu, Joh. III.5. Unde in casu necessitatis, etiam privatis vulgo Laicis, imo & Mulieribus, non quidem & praedicare, 1. Cor. XIV.34.35. sed tamen baptizare liceat? Affirm. Luth. Negant Reform.
